name: Legaltech Hub: A Directory and Analysis Source on AI in Legal
title: Legaltech Hub: A Directory and Analysis Source on AI in Legal
answer: Legaltech Hub is a research database and publishing platform covering legal technology and AI vendors, with topic pages, product profiles, industry surveys and explanatory guides. Its most useful single finding is its own count: as of the end of September 2026, its directory listed 1,416 generative AI solutions from 1,117 providers across 19 categories, giving readers a quantified map of a crowded market before they evaluate individual tools.

sections.body: Legaltech Hub publishes at legaltechnologyhub.com and describes itself as a catalogue and analysis service for legal technology. The pages read span several formats: topic pages on applied AI consultancies and on AI deployment, vendor product pages such as Consilio's Guided AI Review and Conga's CLM AI, news and insight articles, a multi-part Simple Guide to Legal AI, and an industry analysis report on European law firm AI adoption drawn from the 2026 Legaltech Hub and Lexpo European AI Survey. Some material, including an in-depth comparison of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity, sits behind an LTH Premium subscription. The directory figures are stated as of the end of September 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The site's central claim is quantitative: as of the end of September 2026 its directory held 1,416 solutions incorporating generative AI from 1,117 providers across 19 categories, and it has built an interactive map of those solutions and categories. Its topic pages describe two adjacent markets. Applied AI consultancies help firms and legal departments assess where AI adds value, evaluate vendors, build or fine-tune models for document review, research and data extraction, and then support training, adoption and tuning, with many now extending into AI strategy, governance, policy development, use case approval and bias or compliance auditing. A separate deployment category covers the oversight layer: verifying output against a source of record, guardrails blocking privileged or restricted content, enforcing outside counsel guidelines and ethical walls, monitoring usage by user, matter, tool and use case, governed access to firm content, synthetic data for testing, and registries, risk classification and compliance documentation for the EU AI Act, ISO 42001 and GDPR. Product pages describe specific tools, including Consilio's Guided AI Review with human AI Guides averaging over eight years of experience, and Conga's CLM AI, which extracts data from contracts, covers 1,350 or more provisions across multiple languages, flags high-risk clauses and traces its roots to Contract Wrangler, acquired on 17 August 2021. The European survey report argues firms have moved past whether to adopt AI, and introduces a seven-stage Legal AI Transformation Framework running from strategy and governance to transformation.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The directory count of 1,416 generative AI solutions from 1,117 providers across 19 categories, as of the end of September 2026, is the source's headline number. Consilio states its AI and document review professionals average over eight years of experience. Conga states its CLM AI covers 1,350 or more provisions across multiple languages and dates its technology to the Contract Wrangler acquisition on 17 August 2021. The European survey report introduces a seven-stage Legal AI Transformation Framework. The site also reports Relativity rebranding RelativityOne to Relativity aiR in September, launching Relativity claiR in August, acquiring Gavel in June and releasing an MCP Connector in May, and NetDocuments building its strategy around a Legal Context Graph launched in May.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader tracking AI in legal, this source works as a map before it works as an opinion. The directory count and category map give a sense of scale and segmentation that individual vendor announcements cannot, while the topic pages on applied AI consulting and on AI deployment describe the service and oversight layers that sit around the tools themselves. The European survey adds adoption and governance evidence from law firms, and the product pages show how vendors position specific capabilities such as contract extraction, risk flagging and human-guided review. The Simple Guide series serves readers who need terminology before analysis.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Legal

sections.body: Much of the site is directory and vendor-supplied product description rather than independent testing, so capability claims come from the providers themselves. The most detailed comparison, covering OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Perplexity on use cases, research capability, pricing, confidentiality and privilege, is available only to LTH Premium subscribers. The directory figures are a snapshot dated to the end of September 2026 and will age quickly in a market this active. The European survey report is summarised here rather than reproduced in full, and the guide series is introductory by design.
